rationale: Wikipedia Interval (mathematics) supplies every component semantically: the bounded forms (a,b), [a,b], [a,b), (a,b]; the unbounded forms (a,inf), [a,inf), (-inf,b), (-inf,b], (-inf,inf); the open/closed/half-open naming by whether written endpoints are included; boundedness; and the length b-a of a bounded interval. Lebl, Basic Analysis I, sect. 0.3/1.1 agrees. The item is a reformulation rather than a transcription: it enumerates exactly NINE forms where Wikipedia tabulates eleven cases (it folds the empty and degenerate cases into the same nine presentations), it takes order-convexity as the organising notion and PROVES that each of the nine forms is order-convex rather than asserting the classification, and it fixes a library-specific convention that length attaches to the endpoint presentation and not to the set. Convention deltas: (i) the converse classification (every order-convex subset is empty or one of the nine forms) is true and is explicitly NOT asserted here; (ii) (-inf,inf) counts as both open and closed under the written-endpoint rule, agreeing with the topological reading; (iii) +-inf are declared notation, never elements. Definition, so no proof component (the embedded order-convexity and nondegeneracy verifications are part of the definition's justification, matching the treatment of def-finite-sum and def-integer-power in wave 0).

Wikipedia Monotonic function gives the six notions for sequences (non-decreasing, increasing/strictly increasing, non-increasing, decreasing/strictly decreasing, monotone) and records the very convention fork the item's first remark records, namely that some authors use 'increasing' for the non-strict relation. Lebl sect. 2.2 and Tao sect. 6.3 give the same definitions for sequences. The item is a reformulation: it adds 'eventually monotone' (monotonicity of a tail), and it proves as part of the definition that consecutive comparisons suffice (x_k <= x_{k+1} for all k iff x_j <= x_k for all j <= k), which sources state as a separate observation or leave implicit. Convention delta recorded in the item: the unqualified word 'increasing' is STRICT here, and 'nondecreasing' is always written where equality is allowed. Definition, so no proof component.

Lebl, Basic Analysis I, Thm 2.2.5 states exactly the two claims: a monotone increasing bounded sequence converges to sup{x_n}, and a monotone decreasing bounded sequence converges to inf{x_n}. Wikipedia Monotone convergence theorem, 'Convergence of a monotone sequence of real numbers', states the same for a monotone increasing sequence bounded above and its supremum. Same hypotheses (monotone, bounded on the relevant side, range nonempty), same quantifiers, same direction, same identification of the limit as the supremum/infimum of the range. Rudin Thm 3.14 is the same result in its iff packaging, which this library splits off into cor-monotone-converges-iff-bounded. The local proof is the standard sup-epsilon argument, rewritten into this library's numbered-step format, run twice (once for each claim) instead of deducing claim 2 by reflection, and phrased so that a real epsilon suffices against the rational-epsilon convergence test of def-real-limit: literature-based but materially reformulated, hence ai-altered.

Wikipedia Monotone convergence theorem states the unbounded branch in extended-real form (a monotone increasing sequence not bounded above tends to +infinity, equivalently converges to sup = +infinity); Lebl sect. 2.2 gives the same dichotomy. The item is semantically the same statement but deliberately reformulated away from the extended reals: it never adjoins +infinity to R, and instead reads the conclusion through def-divergence-to-infinity as the pure quantifier statement 'for every M there is K with x_k > M for all k >= K'. It also weakens the hypothesis to the one-sided form actually consumed (range not bounded above, rather than the sequence unbounded), and its own first remark records that the two coincide for a nondecreasing sequence. Convention delta: no extended real line anywhere. The four-step proof is short and locally written from trichotomy plus monotonicity, so ai-generated.

Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Thm 3.14: 'Suppose {s_n} is monotonic. Then {s_n} converges if and only if it is bounded.' Lebl Thm 2.2.5 opens with the same sentence ('A monotone sequence {x_n} is bounded if and only if it is convergent'). Same hypothesis (monotone), same biconditional, same direction, same notion of bounded. Exact source. The local proof is a two-case argument that cites this library's own thm-monotone-convergence and lem-convergent-implies-bounded and translates between the sequence-bounded form |x_k| <= M and the range-bounded form of def-bounded-set, so it is literature-based but materially reformulated: ai-altered.

The nonemptiness half is the standard nested interval theorem (Wikipedia Nested intervals; Rudin Thm 2.38; Lebl sect. 1.4; Bartle-Sherbert Thm 2.5.2), and the uniqueness half is Bartle-Sherbert Thm 2.5.3, which states it as inf{b_n - a_n} = 0. The item merges the two into one statement and strengthens the first: it asserts not merely that the intersection is nonempty but that it EQUALS [sup a_k, inf b_k], and it states the single-point half as a biconditional in the form 'the lengths tend to 0'. The two forms of the length condition agree here because the lengths are nonincreasing under nestedness, but that equivalence is a step the sources do not have to take. Semantically identical to the sourced pair, reformulated and merged, hence ai-altered. The proof is the standard sup/inf argument, restructured so that no Archimedean input is needed (the lengths are handled by the algebra of limits and uniqueness of limits rather than by a 'some length is smaller' argument), so it is adapted rather than followed: ai-altered.

Wikipedia Subsequential limit: 'a subsequential limit of a sequence is the limit of some subsequence' - exactly the definition given here, with the same quantifier structure (there exists a strictly increasing index map whose composite converges to L) and no hypothesis on the sequence. Tao sect. 6.6 gives the same notion under the name 'limit point of a sequence'. The subsequential-limit SET and the notation SL(x) are standard and are named as such in the same source. The terminology remark (cluster point / limit point / accumulation value as synonyms, and the deliberate reservation of 'limit point' for the topological notion about SETS) is a convention record, not a new claim. Definition, so no proof component.

ProofWiki Peak Point Lemma and the Monotone Subsequence Theorem state exactly this: every sequence of real numbers has a monotone subsequence, with no hypothesis on the sequence, proved by the peak dichotomy; Lebl sect. 2.3 is the same. The definition of a peak used here (n is a peak when x_m <= x_n for every m >= n) is the source definition. Exact statement, exact hypotheses, exact conclusion. The PROOF is materially reformulated: the standard argument picks 'the next peak' and 'a later larger term' informally, which is a use of dependent choice; this version defines the successor functions outright as LEAST elements supplied by thm-well-ordering-principle and then builds the index map with thm-recursion, so the lemma is proved choice-free. That is an adaptation of a sourced argument, hence ai-altered.

Wikipedia Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem: 'each bounded sequence in R^n has a convergent subsequence'; Rudin Thm 3.6(b) and Lebl Thm 2.3.8 state the R case verbatim. Same hypothesis (bounded), same conclusion (a convergent subsequence exists), same direction; the item's equivalent phrasing 'the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty' is the same claim through def-subsequential-limit. The proof is the monotone-subsequence route (Wikipedia gives it as an alternative proof), but written here as exactly two citations into lem-peak-monotone-subsequence and cor-monotone-converges-iff-bounded so that the use of completeness is isolated in one named place; that restructuring makes it ai-altered rather than a followed source proof.

Tao, Analysis I, Prop 6.1.17 ('Cauchy sequences are bounded') and Wikipedia Cauchy sequence both state exactly this: every Cauchy sequence of reals is bounded. Same hypothesis, same conclusion, same notion of bounded (there is M with |x_k| <= M at every index). Rudin Thm 3.11(a) is the metric-space form. The proof is the standard division of labour (apply the Cauchy condition at a single epsilon to confine the tail, then take a maximum over the finitely many remaining terms), instantiated at epsilon = 1 and rewritten into numbered steps, with an explicit note that the rational 1 is an admissible test value under the rational-epsilon convention of def-real-limit: literature-based and materially reformulated, hence ai-altered.

Lebl sect. 2.4 and Rudin Thm 3.11(b) state exactly this: if a Cauchy sequence has a subsequence converging to L then the whole sequence converges to L. Same hypotheses (Cauchy, plus one convergent subsequence), same conclusion including the identification of the limit as that subsequence's limit, same direction. Wikipedia Cauchy sequence records the same fact. The proof is the standard epsilon/2 bridge argument recast into numbered steps, with the index-growth fact n_j >= j cited explicitly (lem-index-map-grows) rather than waved at, and with the single bridging index chosen once instead of being made to grow with k: adapted from the sourced argument, hence ai-altered.

Lebl Thm 2.4.5 and Rudin Thm 3.11(c) state exactly this: every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real. Wikipedia Completeness of the real numbers states the same and records that the least-upper-bound property implies it. Same hypothesis, same conclusion, same direction. The proof is the standard three-step route (Cauchy implies bounded; bounded gives a convergent subsequence; a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges), each step delegated to a named item on this page, and rewritten into this library's step format: ai-altered. Recorded for Alpha: the title and the second paragraph of the Statement generalise the conclusion to EVERY complete ordered field, while the three cited lemmas are all stated for R; the generalisation is true and standard but is not carried out on the page. See the findings file, item N1; the classification above is unaffected because both the R form and the complete-ordered-field form are sourced.

Claim 1 is Rudin Thm 3.20(b) ('if |x| < 1 then lim x^n = 0') and Wikipedia Geometric progression records the same convergence/divergence dichotomy by |r|. Claim 2 as stated here, that |r|^k diverges to +infinity for |r| > 1, is the standard divergence half but restricted to the ABSOLUTE VALUES, which is a deliberate correction the sources do not always make explicit: for r < -1 the terms r^k alternate in sign, so they neither converge nor diverge to +infinity, and the item says so. Merging the two claims into one lemma and restricting claim 2 to |r|^k is a reformulation, hence ai-altered. The proof follows the standard Bernoulli-inequality route (Wikipedia Bernoulli's inequality is the named tool) with the reciprocal Archimedean property supplying the thresholds, rewritten into a three-case split (r = 0, 0 < |r| < 1, |r| > 1): adapted, hence ai-altered.

PlanetMath, 'contractive sequence': 'The sequence a_0, a_1, a_2, ... in a metric space (X,d) is called contractive, iff there is a real number r in (0,1) such that for any positive integer n the inequality d(a_n, a_{n+1}) <= r * d(a_{n-1}, a_n) is true.' Specialised to X = R with d(u,v) = |u - v| and reindexed from 0 that is exactly the displayed condition |x_{k+2} - x_{k+1}| <= c |x_{k+1} - x_k| for every k in N with 0 < c < 1, with the same quantifier order (one constant, all indices). Bartle-Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis, sect. 3.5 (Def 3.5.7) is the same definition and is the source the item already cites. Exact statement. The three observations attached to the definition (the constant must not depend on k; any c' in [c,1) is also a constant; constant and eventually constant sequences are contractive) are immediate unfoldings, not new claims. Definition, so no proof component.

PlanetMath contractive sequence: 'If the sequence is contractive, it is a Cauchy sequence', with the displayed bound d(a_m, a_n) < d(a_0, a_1) * r^m / (1-r). Bartle-Sherbert Thm 3.5.8 ('every contractive sequence is a Cauchy sequence, and therefore is convergent') and its Cor 3.5.9 (|x* - x_n| <= C^{n-1}/(1-C) * |x_2 - x_1|) supply claims 2 and 3 verbatim, and claim 1 (|x_{k+1} - x_k| <= c^{k-1}|x_2 - x_1|) is the intermediate estimate inside that proof. The item MERGES the three into one theorem and, because this library indexes sequences from 0 while Bartle-Sherbert index from 1, it adds the explicit hypothesis k >= 1 to claims 1 and 3 and supplies a witness showing both are FALSE at k = 0 (x_0 = 0, x_k = 1 for k >= 1, c = 1/2). That index-boundary hypothesis is the item's own contribution to an otherwise sourced statement, so the merged statement is ai-altered rather than exact. The proof follows the sourced telescoping/geometric-sum route, restructured into an induction for claim 1, a finite-sum estimate for the Cauchy property, and a limit-passage for claim 3: ai-altered. Convention delta: 0-indexing, hence the k >= 1 hypothesis.

Every mathematical claim here is established and recoverable, so this is ai-altered and not ai-generated. Wikipedia Parity (mathematics) states the partition claim 2 packages: every integer is even or odd and never both, and the even and odd integers are enumerated by 2j and 2j+1. Claim 3's sequence is the standard (-1)^k, which the item's own remark identifies. Tao sect. 2.1 is the source for defining such objects by recursion and for the uniqueness clause used. What is local is the PACKAGING, not the mathematics: the item presents the even and odd index maps by the recursions e_{sigma(j)} = sigma(sigma(e_j)) and o_{sigma(j)} = sigma(sigma(o_j)) instead of by the closed forms 2j and 2j+1, and it collects the partition, the sequence, and the values into one lemma so that three items on this page and its companion can cite it instead of rebuilding the recursion. Convention deltas: von Neumann naturals with successor sigma, no arithmetic on N beyond the successor, and disjointness of the two ranges proved through the sequence (s takes 1 on one range and -1 on the other, and 1 != -1) rather than by a parity argument. That disjointness proof is the item's own device, and the four inductions are locally written, so the proof component is ai-generated.

Every mathematical claim in the remark is sourced. Wikipedia Completeness of the real numbers states that the least-upper-bound property implies Cauchy completeness; that Cauchy completeness ALONE does not imply it, the standard witnesses being non-Archimedean ordered fields that are Cauchy complete and not Dedekind complete; that Cauchy completeness TOGETHER WITH the Archimedean property does imply it; that the nested interval property stands in the same relation; and that the complete ordered field is unique up to isomorphism. Wikipedia Archimedean property supplies the reason the sequential forms cannot see the gap, namely elements no sequence of naturals reaches. What is local is the editorial half: which of the two proofs this library records where, why both are kept, and the explicit scope denial that the converse implications are not available at this point in the reading order. That is a statement about this library, not a mathematical claim, and it is exactly the pattern Alpha accepted for rem-metric-axiom-conventions in wave 0. Remark, so no proof component.

The content is the standard textbook observation that closedness cannot be dropped from the nested interval theorem, with the canonical witness (0, 1/n): Wikipedia Nested intervals and the standard course treatments of Rudin Thm 2.38 both record that the intervals must be closed and give this family. The item's own construction is the FALSE-STATEMENT framing: it states the open-interval version as a claim and refutes it, which is a reformulation of a sourced remark rather than a transcription, hence ai-altered. Convention delta: 0-indexed, so the witness is written (0, 1/(k+1)) and the item says so explicitly. The refutation is the standard reciprocal-Archimedean argument rewritten into numbered steps, hence ai-altered.

Wikipedia Cauchy sequence states the exact caution this item refutes - that it is not sufficient for each term to become arbitrarily close to the PRECEDING term - and gives the very witness used here, the sequence sqrt(n), whose consecutive differences tend to 0 while the sequence is unbounded and hence not Cauchy. ProofWiki, 'Sequence of Square Roots of Natural Numbers is not Cauchy', proves that half. The item's construction is the false-statement framing of that sourced caution together with the identity sqrt(k+1) - sqrt(k) = 1/(sqrt(k+1) + sqrt(k)), so it is a reformulation of sourced material: ai-altered. The refutation is written locally from the library's square-root and Archimedean items, with the bound 1/(sqrt(k+1)+sqrt(k)) <= 1/sqrt(k+1) and a squaring comparison, so it is adapted rather than followed: ai-altered.

The refuted claim is the converse of the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, and its falsity is standard: Wikipedia Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem states the implication in one direction only, and the failure of the converse is the routine accompanying observation, since an unbounded sequence can still have a constant subsequence. The claim being refuted is therefore recoverable established mathematics, not an invented proposition, so the statement component is ai-altered. What is local is the particular WITNESS, the interleaving 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 4, ... built from the even and odd index maps of lem-alternating-sequence, and the refutation written around it; no source supplies that construction, so the proof component is ai-generated. Recorded for Alpha as a borderline: an alternative reading tags the whole item by its witness, which would make it ai-generated/trivial - but the item is a load-bearing deps target (cex-unbounded-with-convergent-subsequence cites it), so the statement label must classify the refuted CLAIM, which is sourced.

Wikipedia Methods of computing square roots gives the Heron/Babylonian iteration x_{n+1} = (x_n + S/x_n)/2 and records that for S = 2 from a starting value above sqrt(S) the iterates decrease monotonically to sqrt(S); Wikipedia Square root of 2 gives the same sequence starting from 2 as the standard rational approximation scheme. Same recursion, same starting value, same three conclusions (strictly decreasing, every term above sqrt 2, limit sqrt 2). Exact source. The verification is the standard monotone-plus-bounded-plus-fixed-point argument, but it is written around the specific algebraic identity g_{j+1}^2 - 2 = ((g_j^2 - 2)/(2 g_j))^2, it constructs the sequence through thm-recursion on the set of positives so that the recursion is legitimate before it is used, and it discharges L != 0 explicitly before invoking the quotient case of the algebra of limits: adapted, hence ai-altered.

The nested radical sqrt(2 + sqrt(2 + sqrt(2 + ...))) = 2 and its treatment as the recursion x_{n+1} = sqrt(2 + x_n) - increasing, bounded above by 2, limit the positive root of L^2 = 2 + L - is standard (Wikipedia Nested radical; the same worked example appears throughout the standard monotone-convergence exercise literature). The item is ai-altered rather than exact on two counts: the usual presentation starts at x_1 = sqrt 2, whereas this one starts at x_1 = 1, and the usual presentation passes to the limit directly in the recursion, whereas this one squares first and passes to the limit in (x_{k+1})^2 = 2 + x_k, deliberately avoiding continuity of the square root, which this library has not proved at this point. Convention delta: 0-indexed realisation g_j with g_0 = 1. Both the recursion-theorem construction and the squaring device are locally written, so the proof is ai-altered.

The family [0, 1/n] with intersection exactly {0} is the canonical worked instance of the single-point case of the nested interval theorem and appears with those endpoints in the standard treatments (Wikipedia Nested intervals; the usual course notes accompanying Rudin Thm 2.38). Same family, same conclusion, same reason (the lengths 1/n tend to 0 by the Archimedean property). Exact source. Convention delta: 0-indexed realisation J_j = [0, 1/(j+1)], which the item states explicitly. The verification is written locally against this library's cor-archimedean-reciprocal and thm-nested-interval-property, and it deliberately computes the intersection twice (once by the theorem, once by inspection), so it is adapted: ai-altered.

The sequence (-1)^n (1 + 1/n) is the standard textbook example of a bounded divergent sequence whose subsequential limit set is exactly {-1, 1}, hence limsup 1 and liminf -1; it is used in that role in the standard limsup/liminf treatments (MIT 18.100A Lecture 9, 'Limsup, Liminf, and the Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem'; Lebl sect. 2.3). Same sequence, same three conclusions (bounded with 1 < |x_k| <= 2, divergent, SL = {-1,1}). Exact source. Convention delta: 0-indexed realisation u_j = t_j (1 + 1/(j+1)) with t_j = -s_j, which the item states explicitly and which shifts the sign so that u_0 = x_1. The verification is locally constructed: it routes the sign through lem-alternating-sequence rather than through (-1)^k, and it settles the converse inclusion by taking absolute values (|u_{n_i}| = p_{n_i} -> 1, so |L| = 1) instead of splitting an arbitrary subsequence by parity. That device is the item's own, so the proof is ai-generated.

Positive novelty determination, on the witness. Linear fixed-point iteration u -> (u+1)/3 is an instance of a completely standard family (Wikipedia Fixed-point iteration; Contraction mapping), but no source selects THIS map, this constant, or this arbitrary starting value as its worked example; the map is chosen for this page so that the contraction inequality holds with EQUALITY at every index and c = 1/3 is therefore the smallest admissible constant. That is a bespoke checkable witness, which the AUDIT-WORKFLOW sect. 6 trivial row assigns to ai-generated with generation.role: example, following the wave-0 precedent Alpha upheld for cex-same-cardinality-without-a-canonical-bijection. Truth verified directly and completely from the stated dependencies: x_{k+2} - x_{k+1} = ((x_{k+1}+1) - (x_k+1))/3 = (x_{k+1} - x_k)/3, so |x_{k+2} - x_{k+1}| = (1/3)|x_{k+1} - x_k| exactly, giving contractivity with c = 1/3 in (0,1); thm-contractive-implies-cauchy then gives convergence to some L; the first tail has the same limit, so L = (L+1)/3, i.e. 3L = L+1, i.e. L = 1/2, for every starting value a. The remark's arithmetic also checks: x_1 = (a+1)/3, x_2 = (a+4)/9, so |x_2 - x_1| = |(1-2a)/9| = (2/9)|a - 1/2|. Blast radius nil: zero deps consumers corpus-wide. Recorded for Alpha as a borderline - ai-altered under an instance-of-a-standard-family reading is also defensible, and the label does not affect dependency eligibility here.

The truncated decimal approximations of sqrt 2 as a Cauchy sequence of rationals with no rational limit is the canonical witness for the incompleteness of Q (Wikipedia Completeness of the real numbers; Tao sect. 5.1 uses the same construction as the motivation for building R). Same witness, same conclusion. The item is ai-altered rather than exact because what it ADDS is the view from R - that the same sequence converges in R, with limit sqrt 2 - which the sources treat as the definition of R rather than as a computation about a witness, and because the construction is stated as s_n = k_n/10^n with k_n the largest natural satisfying k_n^2 <= 2 * 10^{2n}, a specific formalisation of 'truncated decimal'. The verification is locally written: the two-sided estimate 0 <= sqrt 2 - s_n < 10^{-n} is turned into convergence by thm-squeeze and lem-geometric-sequence-null, then the rational-limit case is closed by fs-sqrt2-rational. Adapted, hence ai-altered.

The family (0, 1/n) with empty intersection is THE named counterexample showing that closedness cannot be dropped from the nested interval theorem, and it appears with exactly these endpoints in the standard treatments (Wikipedia Nested intervals; the standard course notes on the Nested Intervals Theorem accompanying Rudin Thm 2.38). Same family, same conclusion, same reason. Exact source. Convention delta: 0-indexed realisation J_j = (0, 1/(j+1)), stated in the item. The counterexample section defers the refutation itself to fs-nested-open-intervals-nonempty and records the witness, which is this library's own A/B page structure, so the local argument is adapted: ai-altered.

The family [n, infinity) with empty intersection is THE named counterexample showing that boundedness cannot be dropped from the nested interval theorem, and it appears with exactly these endpoints in the standard treatments (Wikipedia Nested intervals; the standard course notes on the Nested Intervals Theorem; the same pairing with the open-interval counterexample). Same family, same conclusion, same reason (the naturals are cofinal in R, so no real dominates every k). Exact source. The local argument is written against this library's thm-of-archimedean and def-interval, which admits [a, infinity) as one of its nine forms and assigns it no length, so it is adapted: ai-altered.

Wikipedia Cauchy sequence gives exactly this witness for exactly this purpose: the sequence sqrt(n), whose consecutive terms become arbitrarily close while the sequence itself is unbounded and therefore not Cauchy. ProofWiki, 'Sequence of Square Roots of Natural Numbers is not Cauchy', is the same statement proved. Same sequence, same two properties, same conclusion. Exact source. The item's added claim, that sqrt k diverges to +infinity, is the routine sharpening and is proved here from thm-of-archimedean and the monotonicity of squaring. The local argument defers the refutation to fs-consecutive-differences-null-implies-cauchy and proves only the divergence, which is this library's A/B structure: ai-altered.

Positive novelty determination, on the witness. That the converse of Bolzano-Weierstrass fails is established (and is tagged as such on the false statement this item refutes, fs-convergent-subsequence-implies-bounded), but the WITNESS is bespoke: the interleaving 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 4, ... defined by cases on the even/odd partition of N supplied by lem-alternating-sequence, together with the computation that its subsequential limit set is exactly {1}. No source selects this construction; the item builds it from this page's own machinery. That is the bespoke checkable-witness species the AUDIT-WORKFLOW sect. 6 trivial row assigns to ai-generated with generation.role: counterexample, on the wave-0 precedent Alpha upheld. Truth verified directly from the stated dependencies: the definition is total and single-valued because e and o partition N and each is injective; the subsequence along o is constantly 1, hence convergent; for any real M the Archimedean property gives m >= 1 with |M| < m, and y_{e_{m-1}} = m > |M| >= M, so no M bounds |y_n|; and any convergent subsequence meets the range of e only finitely often (its values j+1 exceed every bound), so it is eventually constantly 1 and its limit is 1, giving SL = {1}. Blast radius nil: zero deps consumers corpus-wide. Recorded for Alpha as a borderline - ai-altered under established-knowledge is defensible if Alpha judges the interleaving itself to be canonical.

Positive novelty determination, on the witness. That strictly decreasing gaps are strictly weaker than a uniform contraction constant is the standard caution attached to the contractive definition (Bartle-Sherbert sect. 3.5; Wikipedia Contraction mapping), but the WITNESS is bespoke: the recursion x_1 = 1, x_{k+1} = x_k + 1/x_k is a known recurrence with known asymptotics, and no source selects it to separate 'each gap smaller than the last' from 'contractive'. The construction, the induction g_j^2 >= 1 + 2j, and the divergence argument are written for this page. That is the bespoke checkable-witness species the AUDIT-WORKFLOW sect. 6 trivial row assigns to ai-generated with generation.role: counterexample. Truth verified directly from the stated dependencies: g takes values in {u : u >= 1}, so every gap d_j = 1/g_j is positive and the sequence strictly increases; 0 < g_j < g_{j+1} gives 0 < d_{j+1} < d_j, so the gaps strictly decrease; g_{j+1}^2 = g_j^2 + 2 + 1/g_j^2 > g_j^2 + 2 gives g_j^2 >= 1 + 2j by induction, so for any M the Archimedean n with |M|^2 < n yields g_n^2 >= 1 + 2n > n > |M|^2 and hence g_k >= g_n > M for all k >= n, i.e. divergence to +infinity; a convergent sequence is bounded, so no contraction constant can exist by thm-contractive-implies-cauchy. The remark's ratio computation also checks: d_{j+1}/d_j = g_j/g_{j+1} = g_j^2/(g_j^2 + 1) < 1 and tends to 1. Blast radius nil: zero deps consumers corpus-wide. Recorded for Alpha as a borderline - ai-altered is defensible if Alpha judges the recurrence itself to carry the claim.
